data.title: Jeremy Pope joins ViiV in spreading 'PrEP Wisdom'
data.description:
ViiV Healthcare has tapped a new mind for its “PrEP Wisdom” campaign, with Tony Award-winning actor and fashion icon Jeremy Pope joining in on the education and awareness messaging around long-acting injectable pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) options. 

The campaign and its associated website launched in June with “RuPaul’s Drag Race” judge Michelle Visage, who signed on to encourage people to get “PrEP wise” and make informed decisions about long-acting injectable options for HIV prevention. Pope spreads the same message in his new spots, which will reach digital, broadcast, cable, and social platforms, according to ViiV. 

In one 15-second video, Pope is hanging on a brightly colored porch with friends. 

“A good kiki? That’s where the truth comes out,” he says to the camera. “With injectable PrEP options, the truth is there are differences in addition to the dosing schedules.”

Culturally resonant slang terms like “kiki,” which has its roots in Black LGBTQ ballroom culture, are used throughout the campaign. ViiV hopes this kind of language can “cut through the clutter” and prompt its audience to “stop and pause for a minute and pay attention to the messages of the campaign,” head of U.S. ViiV enterprise communications Bithiah Lafont told Fierce in a recent interview. 

HIV disproportionately impacts Black communities in the U.S., according to the CDC, and recent research points to a high unmet need for PrEP in Black men and women. Across the U.S. overall, only 25% of the 2.2 million people who might benefit from PrEP are currently utilizing it, ViiV has said.  

After Gilead Sciences launched Truvada, the first FDA-approved PrEP medication, in 2012, the market was dominated by daily oral options for nearly a decade. That changed in 2021, when ViiV Healthcare's Apretude became the first FDA-approved long-acting injectable PrEP medication. Gilead expanded the market further last year with Yeztugo, a twice-yearly injectable PrEP option.

Related

ViiV Healthcare launches ‘PrEP Wisdom’ campaign to boost awareness of long-acting HIV prevention meds

Much of the buzz around long-acting injectable options has centered on the dosing schedule each can offer, but ViiV and “PrEP Wisdom” look to draw attention to other factors that could play into choice in PrEP. The campaign website encourages people to ask their doctor about potential injection-site reactions, medicine interactions and other considerations that can determine “an option that fits your lifestyle and goals.”  

Pope has been a “great advocate” for the campaign, Lafont said. “Lending his voice and lending his time to this has really boosted our ability to get conversation out to different communities.”

ViiV designed the campaign website with bright colors and playful fonts to make it feel less like a traditional pharma ad, Lafont said. Since its June launch, the site has sparked conversations online and generated social media engagement, supporting the campaign's broader goal of driving behavior change.

“A lot of the change that we’re hoping to see is going to be reflected in those conversations that people are having with their providers,” Lafont explained. “We know that PrEP is one of the best ways for people to prevent HIV, and we also know that the majority of people who could benefit from PrEP are not taking PrEP, and largely that's because either their doctors are not having the conversation or they're not asking their doctors about it.”

She emphasized the importance of informed conversations about PrEP options as the number of long-acting treatments available continues to grow.

As the first company to enter the long-acting injectable PrEP market, ViiV has seen attitudes toward injectable treatments evolve. Lafont pointed to the growing popularity of injectable GLP-1 drugs for diabetes and obesity as one factor contributing to greater acceptance of injectable medicines. Despite that shift, she emphasized that PrEP uptake must increase to make meaningful progress in combating the HIV epidemic.

ViiV, which is majority-owned by GSK and focuses exclusively on HIV, has seen strong growth in its long-acting injectable portfolio. GSK reported that long-acting injectables accounted for 80% of its HIV sales growth in the third quarter, with Apretude generating £403 million ($538.7 million) in sales through the first nine months of 2026. Meanwhile, Gilead's competing Yeztugo brought in $702 million over the same period.

GSK has long maintained that Yeztugo won't dominate the long-acting injectable PrEP market, with executives citing potential tolerability concerns, injection-site nodules and drug interactions as factors that could limit its appeal. The rival drug “definitely won’t be for everyone,” GSK's president of corporate development, David Redfern, said in early 2025.

Still, both companies share a mission to increase U.S. PrEP uptake and normalize conversations around HIV prevention. Gilead recently targeted Hispanic and Latino communities in its “Ahorita Mismo" campaign, while ViiV told prospective HIV treatment or PrEP users to “Do It For Future You” in a recent multichannel campaign.

data.title: Eli Lilly forces compounding rival to shed weight loss claims
data.description:
Eli Lilly has successfully challenged Good Life Meds’ claims about the health benefits and personalization of a compounded tirzepatide product.  

Lilly, which sells the GLP-1/GIP drug tirzepatide as Mounjaro and Zepbound, challenged the telehealth provider’s claims through BBB National Programs’ National Advertising Division (NAD). The drugmaker, the only provider of FDA-approved tirzepatide products, disputed Good Life’s claims about the effect of the compounded drug on body weight, blood sugar, energy and lean muscle. 

After assessing Good Life’s response to the challenge, the NAD recommended that the company stop making the express health benefit and personalization claims challenged by Lilly and modify its ads to remove unsupported implied claims about safety, efficacy and personalization. 

Good Life's response to Lilly’s challenge included substantial clinical literature on tirzepatide, information about additive ingredients and real-world evidence, including a Gallup survey and retrospective cohort studies. Yet the NAD found the literature largely concerned Lilly's FDA-approved products. Neither the Gallup survey nor the cohort studies examined Good Life's compounded tirzepatide, the NAD said. 

Given those limitations, the NAD ruled that Good Life lacked a reasonable basis for the challenged express health-benefit claims. The NAD recommended that Good Life avoid conveying unsupported claims that its compounded drug is safe and effective for the challenged benefits and offers significant efficacy and weight-loss results. 

Good Life voluntarily and permanently discontinued some express and implied claims during the inquiry. The claims related to clinical results, benefits, ingredients, safety and the sourcing of compounded tirzepatide. In its advertiser statement, Good Life said it disagrees with many aspects of the NAD’s decision but will comply with the recommendations. 

The case is the latest in a series of challenges that Lilly and Novo have brought against companies providing compounded copies of their GLP-1 drugs. Lilly won a case against Noom in May, and over the past year Novo has successfully challenged claims made by Fletcher Family Medical Center, Regen Doctors and Willow Health Services.

data.title: The Oral GLP-1 Tracker: Foundayo's record, Wegovy pill's rebound
data.description:
With the recent launches of Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill and Eli Lilly’s Foundayo, the obesity market has started to shift toward oral GLP-1 drugs. While Novo leverages its first-mover advantage with the familiar Wegovy brand, Lilly is betting that the freedom from strict fasting and water requirements can give Foundayo an edge.

Each week, Fierce Pharma’s Oral GLP-1 Tracker will leverage analysts’ notes and IQVIA data to monitor prescription trends and shifting market shares as these two titans vie to become the go-to oral weight-loss solution for millions.

UPDATED: Nov. 6, 2026

Heading into Halloween weekend, both Novo and Lilly saw scripts for their oral obesity medicines tick up. 

In its 30th launch week, Lilly’s Foundayo racked up roughly 65K prescriptions, seemingly topping a more than 64K-script record set during week 25 of the rollout, according to IQVIA data cited by Jefferies. Still, the medicine’s performance pales in comparison to Novo’s Wegovy pill at week 30 of its own launch, when the semaglutide tablet reeled in roughly 173K scripts. 

For the last weekly period, the Wegovy pill charted a 0.5% script increase—or around 8K new prescriptions—to land at around 184K total. That’s roughly on par with the height of the pill’s script performance in 2026 so far and marked a rebound from roughly 183K in the prior week. 

Novo reported earlier this week that the Wegovy pill generated 5.39 billion Danish kroner (nearly $811 million) in third quarter sales. Over the same period, Lilly reported $184 million in sales of Foundayo. 

On an analyst call, Novo’s EVP of U.S. operations, Jamey Millar, resurfaced caveats with the data IQVIA is using to track the oral GLP-1 launches, arguing that Novo boasts “a much more extensive ecosystem of partners for Wegovy” than Lilly, and that those partners “don’t report to IQVIA in absolute terms.” 

“So we’ve consistently seen a lower capture rate for Wegovy pill than the competitive oral product,” he suggested. 

Based on the latest weekly metrics, Lilly holds a little more than a 26% share of the overall oral obesity market compared to Novo’s nearly 74%, the Jefferies team said in its note. 

UPDATED: Oct. 30, 2026

Prescriptions for Eli Lilly's Foundayo and Novo's Wegovy pill ticked back up last week, although neither matched previous records.

Foundayo enjoyed 63,110 total scripts in its 29th week of launch, still shy of its 64,268-script record set in week 25, according IQVIA data cited by Citi. 

The Wegovy pill's roughly 183K scripts also came slightly below the 184K height it had briefly reached five weeks ago. During the week, the oral version of Novo's obesity med constituted 36% of all Wegovy scripts.

Approximately 4 in 10 patients starting an oral obesity medicine choose Foundayo, and the number of new Foundayo patients in the third quarter doubled from the previous quarter, Lilly's CFO said on the company's Q3 earnings call Thursday.

In Q3, Foundayo sales reached $184 million, including $124 million from the U.S., missing consensus estimates by $50 million, according to a Jefferies note. Still, Lilly's stock price jumped during Thursday's earnings report, "which to us suggests investors are increasingly focusing on the breadth and depth of [Lilly]'s obesity franchise rather than near-term Foundayo [numbers]," Jefferies' analysts said. Sales from both of Lilly's tirzepatide products, Mounjaro and Zepbound, came in above Wall Street's projections during Q3.

UPDATED: Oct. 23, 2026

Last week’s federal holiday, Columbus Day, led to an unsurprising dip for prescriptions of both Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill and Eli Lilly’s oral GLP-1 rival Foundayo in the U.S. 

In the prior-week reporting period, Novo’s Wegovy pill saw prescriptions fall slightly to around 173K versus the 173.5K tallied the week ending Oct. 9, according to Citi and Jefferies analysts, both of whom leverage prescribing data from IQVIA. 

For that same period, prescriptions of Eli Lilly’s GLP-1 pill Foundayo slipped around 4% week over week to 58K. 

The minor reversal for both drugs shouldn’t come as a surprise, given that national holidays are liable to impact weekly prescribing trends. 

Looking at the broader oral GLP-1 market, Lilly’s share presently sits a little higher than 25%, according to the Jefferies team, while Novo holds a nearly 75% piece of the pie. 

Meanwhile, as Novo and Lilly vie over the ever-important U.S. obesity market, the GLP-1 opportunity taking shape across other massive countries like China, India and Brazil could grow from $6.6 billion now to a whopping $22 billion by the middle of the next decade, according to a new J.P. Morgan estimate reported by Reuters Friday. 

UPDATED: Oct. 16, 2026

The previous week was rather uneventful for the two oral GLP-1 drugs as Americans geared up for another national holiday, Columbus Day.

Total prescriptions for Novo's Wegovy pill dipped about 3% sequentially to approximately 173.5K last week. Again, the script number was the result of a compromise between Citi's reported 173K and Jefferies' 174K, both referencing IQVIA.

Meanwhile, Lilly's Foundayo scripts ticked up about 4% to 60,151, still shy of the small molecule's previous record of 64,268.

In the broader obesity market, Lilly's Zepbound remained the leader with about 801.8K total scripts, relatively flat week over week. All Wegovy scripts across its injectable and oral forms trended 2.5% downward and landed at about 492.6K, according to Citi.

Earlier this week, drug regulators at the European Medicines Agency recommended a marketing authorization in the European Union for Foundayo for both weight management and Type 2 diabetes in adults. The European Commission is expected to sign off on the approval in a few weeks. 

UPDATED: Oct. 9, 2026

Prescriptions for Lilly's Foundayo and Novo's Wegovy pill pulled back a little during the last week. 

In its 26th week of launch, Foundayo achieved 57,920 total scripts, down 9.9% sequentially, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. 

For oral Wegovy, Citi said IQVIA recorded roughly 179K scripts, while Jefferies quoted 180K. To reconcile the discrepancy between the two numbers, we used 179.5K, which translates into a 1.4% weekly decline.

In fact, scripts for all major GLP-1s declined last week across diabetes and obesity care, save for Lilly's Zepbound KwikPen, a prefilled injection pen that delivers four fixed weekly doses of tirzepatide, according to Jefferies. Overall Zepbound scripts dipped below 800K in a 0.8% decrease sequentially, just as Novo's total Wegovy scripts fell 2.7% to 505.5K, according to Citi.

Based on the numbers, Jefferies now models $208 million for Foundayo sales in the third quarter, which the team noted is in line with consensus.

UPDATED: Oct. 2, 2026

Eli Lilly's Foundayo is showing clearer signs of acceleration. Total prescriptions for the oral GLP-1 receptor agonist surged about 21% to 64,268 during last week, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. That haul came off a 13% sequential increase the week before that.

"We're seeing early signs of growth in Q3 for Foundayo," Jefferies analysts wrote in an Oct. 2 note.

Recent expansion of Foundayo could be attributed to a direct-to-consumer ad first aired in late August featuring Martha Stewart, as well as the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program which, as of July, offers eligible seniors GLP-1 obesity drugs at a $50 monthly copay.

Meanwhile, Novo's Wegovy pill scripts appear stuck at just above $180K. Except for a Labor Day holiday lull, total weekly scripts for the oral semaglutide product have hovered between 181K and 184K over the past five weeks, including 182K last week, according to Citi.

It's worth noting that Foundayo took 25 weeks to reach what the Wegovy pill achieved in just seven weeks in terms of total scripts. But the gap between the two drugs is closing. As Jefferies noted, Lilly owned 26% of the oral obesity market as of last week, versus a little less than 23% in the previous two weeks.

Overall, Lilly's Zepbound remains the obesity market leader with total scripts of 805.7K, up 2.3% sequentially, according to Citi. Novo's total Wegovy scripts for the pill and the injectable were down 0.6% sequentially to a 519.6K.

At the European Association for the Study of Diabetes annual meeting in Milan earlier this week, both Lilly and Novo rolled out multiple data sets touting the blood-sugar, weight-loss, cardiovascular benefits of their GLP-1 programs amid a wave of potential challengers.

UPDATED: Sept. 25, 2026

Total prescriptions for both Eli Lilly's Foundayo and Novo's Wegovy pill have bounced back following a holiday dip and reached new records. Weekly scripts for the Wegov pill jumped 14% sequentially to about 184K, compared with its previous high of 183K, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. Foundayo climbed 13% to cross 50K for the first time, reaching 53,321.

Foundayo now captures about 1 out of 3 new starts for oral GLP-1 obesity drugs, and “that’s growing week over week,” Lilly CEO David Ricks told CNBC in an interview this week. 

As Leerink Partners analysts noted in a Sept. 23 note, effective Sept. 1, Lilly cut the initial-dose pricing for Foundayo 0.8 mg, 2.5 mg and 5.5 mg to $149, $149 and $199 per month for self-pay patients, respectively. The company framed the promotion as an elasticity experiment and as a push to the first maintenance dose, according to the Leerink note.

As Jefferies analysts pointed out in a Sept. 25 note, the majority of Foundayo scripts seem to be cash pay, with about 80% of patients still on starting doses.

Based on the IQVIA data so far, the Jefferies team estimated U.S. Foundayo revenues of $203 million in the third quarter, slightly lower than the $209 million consensus projection. 

Broadly speaking, Lilly yielded 0.6 percentage point of its obesity market share to Novo during the previous week, but still maintained its share level above 60%, according to Citi. 

In the recently launched Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program, Lilly is capturing 7 out of 10 patients, with many on its Zepbound, Ricks told CNBC. Foundayo, according to Ricks, is attracting Medicare patients looking for convenience but not necessarily a huge weight-loss effect. 

UPDATED: Sept. 18, 2026

As expected, the past U.S. Labor Day holiday took a toll on obesity drugs' prescription numbers. According to IQVIA data cited by Citi, weekly scripts for Novo's Wegovy pill dropped roughly 12% sequentially to about 161K for the last week. The decline for Foundayo was modest, at just 1%, as the Lilly drug still managed to rake in more than 47K scripts. 

Lilly this week said Foundayo captured more than 30% of new patients in the U.S. market for oral obesity ​treatments, Reuters reported. 

Citing Bloomberg Symphony data, Jefferies analysts suggested in a Friday note that Foundayo's recent acceleration "has been driven primarily by retail/commercial channels."

Elsewhere, Lilly's total Zepbound scripts were down 8.5% week over week, but the GIP/GLP-1 drug expanded its market share by 0.4% versus Novo's Wegovy franchise, whose scripts decreased 10% during the period.

UPDATED: Sept. 11, 2026

Both Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill and Eli Lilly’s Foundayo saw their highest total prescriptions so far over the past week as the companies’ oral obesity battle continues to play out.  

According to IQVIA data cited by Citi, the Wegovy pill reached an approximate 183K total scripts for the most recent reporting period, versus 181K the week prior. Foundayo, for its part, climbed nearly 8% to reach 47.5K scripts. Citi analysts emphasized that IQVIA may still be missing some Foundayo prescriptions made through telehealth channels. 

Meanwhile, using the last four weeks as a guide, total GLP-1 prescriptions have increased by 5.4%, compared to a 6.8% decline the prior year, the Citi team said. Citi analysts attributed the 12-percentage-point swing to the expansion of oral GLP-1 therapies, which is likely broadening access to the class and drawing in new patients.  

Across the broader landscape, Lilly’s tirzepatide currently holds a nearly 57% share of the total GLP-1 market, compared to around 49.5% last year, while Novo’s semaglutide has stayed relatively flat at a 37% share, the analysts added.  

UPDATED: Sept. 4, 2026

Total prescriptions for Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill and Eli Lilly's Foundayo both grew over the past week, reaching roughly 181K (+3%) and 44K (+8%), IQVIA data showed, as cited by Citi. Both numbers are the two meds' highest so far. 

While Foundayo has yet to catch up with the Wegovy pill, the market share gap between the two oral drugs is slowly narrowing. According to an Aug. 28 Jefferies note based on data the previous week, Foundayo's share of new prescriptions (NRx), which exclude refills, was 21.5% in the oral obesity market.

Back to the most recent week, the Wegovy pill's position within the Wegovy family remained stable at 35%, as total Wegovy scripts increased 2.7% sequentially to 513.5K. During the same period, Lilly's Zepbound scripts climbed 1.6% to a little fewer than 772K.  

UPDATE: Aug. 28, 2026

Twenty weeks into its launch, Eli Lilly's Foundayo has finally exceeded 40,000 in weekly prescriptions, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. The oral GLP-1 drug posted 40,862 scripts last week, bouncing back from a small dip the week prior. Still, the drug's scripts level is no match for the roughly 57K that Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill garnered at week 6 of its own launch.

In its 33rd week of launch, the Wegovy pill booked roughly 175K scripts, slightly down from 176K, per IQVIA. The share of the oral version of semaglutide in all Wegovy obesity scripts was flat week over week at 35%. All told, across the pill and the injectable, Wegovy's weekly scripts were a little over 500K, down 0.8% sequentially.

As Jefferies analysts observed in an Aug. 21 note, Wegovy has been relatively flat since the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program began July 1.

Overall, the roughly 60%-40% obesity market share split between Lilly and Novo remained stable, as Lilly's Zepbound held its ground as the most popular drug.

UPDATE: Aug. 21, 2026

After a one-week hiccup, Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill regained its momentum last week with its largest prescription rate since it was launched in January. There were more than 176,000 prescriptions for the pill in the period, according to data gathered by IQVIA and cited in a note by Citi. 

The oral treatment now accounts for 35% of total Wegovy prescriptions, which is up from 33% the previous week, analysts from Citi said in their weekly update to investors.

Meanwhile, Eli Lilly’s oral GLP-1 Foundayo, which had been on a steady five-week climb, backtracked, with a drop-off from 38,928 prescriptions in the prior period to 36,620 in the latest week.

The movements for the two oral treatments contributed to overall market share adjustments for the companies' diabetes and obesity medicines. While Lilly made a 0.1% gain to 56.7%, Novo increased its market share by 0.3% to 37.1%.  

UPDATE: Aug. 14, 2026

Despite its leading position in the oral GLP-1 market, Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill seems to be hitting a market share ceiling. For months now, shares of total prescriptions for Wegovy pill within the entire Wegovy franchise have struggled to break through the one-third mark.

While share of oral semaglutide within all Wegovy scripts hit 35% in our previous update, it fell back to 33% last week, as Wegovy pill scripts dropped to about 163K, down from a high of roughly 172K the week prior, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. 

Total Wegovy scripts, including the original injectable, declined 1.1% sequentially to about 495.5K. As a result, Novo yielded about 0.7 percentage point in obesity market share to Eli Lilly's Zepbound last week based on the IQVIA data. The split stood at 39.9% and 60.1% between Novo and Lilly.

Meanwhile, Lilly's Foundayo continued its upward trajectory with 38,928 total scripts, representing another step up from its previous record of 34,219 set the week prior.

UPDATE: Aug. 7, 2026

Prescriptions for Eli Lilly's Foundayo continue to build, jumping 16% sequentially to 34,219 the previous week, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. The oral GLP-1 med has been on a roll lately as it appears to celebrate four weeks of consecutive growth in total scripts. However, as Citi noted, there's still a potential gap in IQVIA's capture of telehealth data, and it's not clear how much of the scripts growth was from IQVIA getting better at including those data, or, if the actual growth was much faster in telehealth channels.

This week, Lilly's reported Foundayo sales for the second quarter—$98 million in total, including $67 million in the U.S.—disappointed many. As CEO David Ricks noted on an earnings call, Lilly began broad direct-to-consumer marketing to raise consumer awareness after securing commercial access across the three major pharmacy benefit managers in June. Besides, The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program went live on July 1, offering coverage for certain weight-loss medications, including Foundayo, for a $50 copayment per month. Ilya Yuffa, president of Lilly USA and global customer capabilities, said the company is "starting to see an inflection point on Foundayo now."

As for Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill, total scripts recorded by IQVIA have been largely flat with small upticks in the past two weeks, having reached roughly 172K in the previous week. The oral version of semaglutide now makes up 35% of total Wegovy scripts, which take up about 40.6% of the U.S. obesity market share, as Lilly's Zepbound remains the leader. 

UPDATE: July 31, 2026

The small inflection point we noticed two weeks ago regarding Eli Lilly's Foundayo does not appear to be a flash in the pan. Weekly total prescriptions for the small molecule reached 29,388, a new high for the oral GLP-1 receptor agonist after three weeks of consecutive growth, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. 

As IQVIA may be missing some scripts from telehealth channels, we will get a clearer picture of Foundayo's launch progress when Lilly reports its second-quarter earnings on Wednesday, Aug. 5. Analysts at Jefferies have been modeling $71 million in U.S. sales for the quarter based on IQVIA data.

Meanwhile, Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill remains far ahead in the oral GLP-1 race with total scripts also hitting a new record of about 171,700, according to Citi. The number represents 1.1% growth from its previous best recorded during the prior week.

Coincidentally, the entire GLP-1 class also saw its total scripts grow 1.1% sequentially across diabetes and obesity uses. Lilly's Zepbound regained some lost ground with total scripts up 1.9% week over week. That's compared to Wegovy, which now makes up 40.6% of the obesity market after a 0.2% sequential decline in total scripts. 

Novo reports earnings on the same day as Lilly, Aug. 5.

UPDATE: July 24, 2026

After a post-holiday lull, prescriptions for GLP-1s have more than bounced back. Weekly prescriptions for Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill and Eli Lilly's Foundayo reached new highs during the previous week, collecting 169,800 and 26,760, respectively, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. The two oral drugs' previous records were about 161.5K and 24.3K, respectively. 

Other GLP-1 drugs also enjoyed a boost, as total GLP-1 scripts across obesity and diabetes increased 6.6% sequentially, according to Citi.

From the obesity front, scripts for Lilly's Zepbound rose 7.7% sequentially to about 710K. The GLP-1/GIP dual agonist conceded 0.6 percentage points of market share to Novo but remains ahead of the game with a 58.9% share. That's compared to a 10.5% week-over-week scripts expansion for Novo's Wegovy, which mounted to about 495.5K. In that basket, about 34% belonged to Wegovy pill.

UPDATE: July 17, 2026

Following the Independence Day holiday, the overall GLP-1 market was down 5.1% week over week as measured by total prescriptions across obesity and diabetes uses, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi.

In the obesity field specifically, total scripts for Eli Lilly's Zepbound shrank by 3.1% sequentially to a little below 660K, while Novo Nordisk's Wegovy dipped 4.4% to about 448.5K.

Against this backdrop, Lilly's oral Foundayo seemed to enjoy a small inflection point, with a total 24,303 scripts notably breaking away from its roughly 20K level in the prior five weeks.  

Meanwhile, joining the bigger trend, Wegovy pill scripts dropped to 147.5K during the week, versus about 153K the prior week or 161.5K at its peak. But the contribution of the oral version to the overall Wegovy scripts remained stable at around a third, per Citi's note. 

UPDATE: July 10, 2026

The launch of Eli Lilly’s Foundayo remains “muted,” with weekly prescriptions flat over the last five weeks, analysts from Jefferies said in a July 10 note. The analysis is based on data collected by IQVIA.

In the 13th week of Foundayo’s launch, IQVIA reported 19,550 prescriptions, down for the third straight week after peaking at Week 10 with 21,648 prescriptions. The figure also comes in significantly shy of the Week 13 launch of Novo’s Wegovy pill (more than 105K scripts) and Lilly’s injected obesity treatment Zepbound (59K), but ahead of Novo’s injected Wegovy (13K).

Meanwhile, weekly scripts for Wegovy pill ticked slightly upward sequentially to about 153K, although they still lag behind the drug’s peak of more than 161K.

Jefferies points out that CVS was the last of the big three PBMs to provide coverage of Foundayo, starting on June 1. By contrast, Wegovy had full coverage at the first week of its launch.

While Jefferies’ $71 million quarterly sales projection for Foundayo sits significantly below Wall Street consensus of $130 million, the team still believes that the Lilly med can reach the consensus revenue estimate of $1.2 billion for 2026.

UPDATE: July 6, 2026

For a month now, weekly prescriptions for Eli Lilly's Foundayo have been hovering at around 20,000. In other words, three months into its market debut, the non-peptide GLP-1 receptor agonist was still at the same script level that Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill had achieved in two to three weeks post-launch.

For the week ended on June 26, Foundayo's total scripts dipped about 4% sequentially to 19,830, according to IQVIA data cited by Jefferies. During the same period, scripts were also down about 2% for oral Wegovy, reaching about 149,000.

In a July 4 report, Jefferies analysts modeled about $71 million in U.S. sales during Foundayo's debut quarter from April to June, versus the team's previous estimate of $85 million in a June 26 report. Wall Street's consensus currently has the number at $130 million. To reach its estimate, Jefferies used an illustrative calculation based on the IQVIA data, with certain assumptions regarding pricing, dosing and stocking.

While Lilly still lags Novo on the oral GLP-1 battlefield, the Indianapolis pharma has maintained a majority 59.5% share of the overall obesity market, according to IQVIA's prescription data.  

As Novo's injectable Wegovy gained about 0.2% scripts (roughly 500) to reach 315,000 for the period, Lilly's Zepbound expanded by 1%, including 375,000 (+3,500) from Zepbound autoinjector and 289,000 (+2,000) from Zepbound DTC Vial+KwikPen.

UPDATE: June 29, 2026

Likely thanks to the Juneteenth federal holiday, prescriptions for both Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill and Eli Lilly's Foundayo were lower compared with their highest. For the week ended on June 19, Foundayo logged 20,594 total scripts, down from 21,648 the prior week, according to IQVIA data cited by Jefferies. 

For oral Wegovy, the numbers were about 152,000 for the June 19 week, a roughly 9,500 (5.9%) decrease from the prior week. 

As Jefferies' analysts noted, most GLP-1 scripts were down or rather flat in their weekly comparisons. Injectable Wegovy added about 1,000 (0.3%) scripts, landing at 315,000. Mounjaro essentially saw no change, at 804,000.

Lilly has previously noted that it takes time to build awareness for Foundayo as a new brand, whereas Novo benefits from familiarity with the Wegovy moniker. 

Meanwhile, Sandoz just announced that the FDA has accepted its generic tirzepatide autoinjector applications, covering all indications of Lilly's Mounjaro and Zepbound. We'll see how the availability of a generic injectable version shakes up the oral market. 

UPDATE: June 18, 2026

Name recognition and "familiarity" with Novo Nordisk's oral Wegovy has contributed to its rapid uptake in its battle with Lilly's oral GLP-1 Foundayo, according to Spherix analyst Jim Hickey, who conducts monthly surveys with doctors who prescribe the treatments. See Fierce's story on Hickey's analysis here.

UPDATE: June 12, 2026

The share of Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill among total Wegovy scripts appears to have reached a plateau, hovering around one-third over the past few weeks. The latest number for the week ended on June 5 was 33%, compared with 30%, 32% and 31% in the prior weeks, according to Citi. 

Meanwhile, the obesity market share split between Wegovy and Eli Lilly's Zepbound has been relatively stable at around 40% to 42%, as the Indianapolis pharma's oral Foundayo makes up only a small portion of the market even though its own scripts continue to build. 

Wegovy's total scripts were up 9.8% on a weekly basis, reaching nearly 484,500. Within this haul, Wegovy pill contributed roughly 159,000, the oral version's highest since its launch. The drug's previous highest was 146,000 before dipping to 134,000 in our last update.

Zepbound's scripts also grew week over week by 9.3%, nearing 667,400 for the week. During the same period, IQVIA tracked slightly shy of 20,000 scripts from Foundayo in its ninth week on the market, compared with nearly 17,000 the prior week. 

Thanks to the expansion of the oral version, Wegovy overall now commands 42.1% of the obesity market. Tracing backwards, its share has been climbing steadily, clocking in at 41.9%, 41.2%, 41.4%, 40.5%, 40.4%, 42.6% and 40.4% in the past few weeks.

UPDATE: June 8, 2026

It took just over five months for Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill to log 3 million total U.S. prescriptions, underscoring “one of the strongest US pharmaceutical launches by volume on record,” the company announced in a June 7 press release. Meanwhile, Eli Lilly’s rival Foundayo has still yet to achieve more than 17,000 prescriptions, according to a June 5 note from Citi analysts.  

Using data from IQVIA, the analysts tracked 16,982 Foundayo prescriptions as of the drug's eighth week on the market since its April launch. However, the Citi team emphasizes that “there may be a gap in telehealth capture,” as Lilly has previously confirmed to the analysts around 20,000 Foundayo scripts since its launch. Foundayo has been floating around this range for several weeks now since hitting 16,698 at week six, the data show.

Meanwhile, Novo’s Wegovy pill was at 73,544 prescriptions by the time it had hit the same eight-week marker in its own launch. The drug had picked up one million prescriptions 12 weeks after launching and nabbed an additional two million prescriptions in the following ten weeks, Novo said in its release. At its three million total, one prescription is filled roughly every five seconds, the company pointed out in its release. 

Either way, IQVIA’s data suggests a preference for oral formulations in the wider GLP-1 market, with oral Wegovy prescriptions now contributing 30% of total Wegovy scripts, according to the Citi analysts. The oral offering may be driving a wider market for the obesity treatments as well, with Novo explaining in its recent release that more than 80% of its new prescriptions for the Wegovy pill come from people new to GLP-1 therapy. 

June 2 findings from Spherix Global Insights second the notion that oral GLP-1 pills are expanding the overall treatment pool and drawing in a “massive wave of new patients,” the company said in an emailed release. In oral Wegovy’s first four weeks on the market earlier this year, 73% of surveyed primary care physician reported prescribing the med, with over 98% who haven’t yet prescribed it planning to within the next six months, Spherix found. 

“Novo Nordisk’s early performance has set an exceptionally high bar for the competition,” Spherix’s gastroenterology franchise head, Jim Hickey, commented.

On a weekly basis, however, total GLP-1 prescriptions were trending downward over the week of June 1, falling 5.7% week-over-week, Citi analysts noted. Other than the continued rollout of Lilly and Novo’s respective weight loss pills, the analysts cited the effect of the Trump administration’s “most favored nation” pricing policies as a key future event that they think could impact total prescriptions. 

UPDATE: June 1, 2026

In its seventh week on the market, which ended May 22, Eli Lilly’s obesity pill Foundayo continued to track below the pace of Novo Nordisk’s rival Wegovy pill at the same point in its launch.

At the same time, analysts at Jefferies and Citi again flagged caveats that could be skewing the numbers, with the Jefferies team espousing confidence that Lilly’s oral GLP-1 can still meet consensus sales projections for both the second quarter and 2026 as a whole. 

Breaking down the numbers, the Jefferies team put seventh-week total Foundayo prescriptions lower versus the previous week at roughly 11,700, with the clarification that the data’s source, IQVIA, had to use a “best-estimate” tally for the latest week’s prescription trends. 

That trend remains “numerically lower” than the course charted by Novo’s Wegovy pill, which racked up an impressive 67,000 prescriptions in its seventh week, although Foundayo’s performance still tracks ahead of Novo’s injectable Wegovy and Lilly’s first obesity incretin med Zepbound at the same point in their respective rollouts, the analyst team said. 

Lilly has suggested it expects the market for oral obesity meds to “develop over time” and has also cited the time needed to build new brand awareness for Foundayo, according to Jefferies, which added that the Lilly pill’s commercial reimbursement “appears to be ramping more slowly” compared to oral Wegovy. Lilly has confirmed that coverage of Foundayo through CVS Caremark, the United States’ biggest PBM, will begin this week. 

Despite those apparent growing pains, the analysts at Jefferies called Foundayo’s ability to meet consensus sales estimates in the near-term and for the full year as “doable.” The analysts currently predict that Lilly’s oral weight loss med will garner $145 million in the second quarter on the way to a $1.6 billion haul for the full year. 

Consensus estimates are tracking for Q2 and full-year Foundayo sales of $136 million and $1.2 billion, respectively, according to Jefferies. 

On that note, analysts at Citi, have repeatedly warned that IQVIA’s prescription data may be failing to account for telehealth referrals, citing comments from Lilly executives on the total patients they were tracking as of the company’s Q1 earnings call. For its part, Citi placed the total number of Foundayo scripts for the week ending May 22 at roughly 16,000, based on the IQVIA stats. 

By comparison, Novo’s Wegovy pill clocked some 146,000 total scripts over that same seven-day stretch, per Citi. Citi once more flagged that Novo’s Wegovy pill is making up a growing portion of overall semaglutide obesity prescriptions, which the team said points to “preferences for oral formulations.”

UPDATE: May 22, 2026

With both Novo Nordisk’s and Eli Lilly’s oral GLP-1s establishing their footing in the U.S. obesity market, the companies’ respective Wegovy pill and orforglipron tablet Foundayo are making their mark on prescription trends for a class previously confined primarily to injectables.

Looking at the past four weeks, total U.S. GLP-1 prescriptions were up 3.6%, compared to 1.8% at the same time last year, analysts at Citi wrote in a Friday note to clients, citing script tracking data from IQVIA. The Citi team attributed that momentum to the ability of Novo’s and Lilly’s new oral launches to “broaden and reshape the market” for obesity incretin drugs.

As of the week ended May 15, IQVIA logged nearly 17,000 prescriptions for Lilly’s Foundayo, which debuted on April 9. As in prior weeks, the Citi analysts caveated that IQVIA’s data may be missing key prescribing stats from telehealth channels, flagging Lilly executives’ comments during an earnings call at the end of last month that there were then roughly 20,000 patients on the new oral therapy.

Conversely, Novo’s Wegovy pill has recorded roughly 142,000 prescriptions as of last week, according to Citi’s note.

In an apparent sign of the new oral option's popularity, the analysts flagged that oral Wegovy now comprises 31% of total prescriptions for the brand, which is otherwise administered as an injection. The Citi team noted that this trend could signal “preferences for oral formulations.”

Meanwhile, scoping out the broader U.S. GLP-1 market over the past four weeks, Lilly’s tirzepatide brand—which includes both Zepbound for obesity and Mounjaro for Type 2 diabetes—now holds a 54.8% share compared to a 47% piece of the pie last year. Novo’s U.S. market share for semaglutide has remained “relatively flat” over that stretch and clocked in at 37.4%, per Citi.

Week over week, total GLP-1 prescriptions were down a little less than 1% in the U.S. Looking at obesity specifically, Citi’s analysts flagged a 2.1% tirzepatide prescription decline versus last week, while Novo’s Wegovy prescriptions tracked at a positive 1.8%.

Aside from both companies' oral GLP-1 launches continuing to add texture to the market, the analysts noted that the effect of the Trump administration’s “most favored nation” pricing policies on Novo’s and Lilly’s drugs could boost overall prescriptions for the class. 

UPDATE: May 15, 2026

Total prescriptions for Eli Lilly’s Foundayo reached 10,248 for the week that ended May 8, up from 7,335 the prior week, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. While still on the rise, Foundayo’s growth pace continued to lag behind that of Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill during the same stage of their launch. 

Wegovy’s total scripts rose by 1.3% week over week to nearly 446,000, as its share in the obesity GLP-1 market climbed 0.1 percentage point to 40.5%, according to Citi.

However, Wegovy’s growth apparently didn’t come from its oral formulation. Wegovy pill scripts landed at about 137,000 for the week, down from roughly 143,000 the prior week, marking the first time that the pill's scripts have fallen since the oral launch in early January.

Scripts from the Wegovy pill made up 31% of total Wegovy scripts for the period, down 2 percentage points from the previous week. Still, Citi analysts argued that this roughly one-third of share “suggests preferences for oral formulations.”

Even as Wegovy gained ground, Lilly’s Zepbound remained the obesity market leader, with 59.5% share, as its nearly 656,000 scripts marked 0.8% growth week over week. 

UPDATE: May 8, 2026

As Eli Lilly’s Foundayo finds its footing on the market, Novo Nordisk’s own Wegovy pill—which got a three-month head start to launch over its rival this year—is starting to illuminate just how significant an oral GLP-1 may be to the lucrative obesity drug landscape. 

In the fourth week since its April 9 debut in the U.S., Lilly’s Foundayo has generated 7,335 total prescriptions, analysts at Citi wrote in a note to clients Friday, citing prescribing stats from IQVIA. 

That ramp-up looks slower on paper than that enjoyed by the Wegovy pill during its initial rollout, but the Citi team cautioned that there may be a gap in IQVIA data linked to telehealth prescriptions for Lilly’s tablet. They pointed to comments from Lilly executives late last week indicating that there were now some 20,000 patients on Foundayo, with the company noting that telehealth platforms were generating some 35% of the oral GLP-1 medicine’s current launch volume. 

The analysts acknowledged that Lilly’s early Foundayo prescription trends “continue to build,” while adding that they “look for further growth to develop the oral competitive market.” 

During its earnings call last week, Lilly added that upcoming coverage secured at major pharmacy benefit managers should come online by the middle of May, providing a likely sizeable tailwind to Foundayo’s trajectory. 

As for Novo, the company logged some 440,410 Wegovy prescriptions on the week that ended May 1, with oral Wegovy now making up 33% of those total obesity referrals, per the Citi analysts, who said that trend could reflect “preferences for oral formulations.”

The update on the oral obesity numbers comes after Novo earlier this week reported that the Wegovy pill generated 2.26 billion Danish kroner (around $355 million) in its first quarter on the U.S. market. 

For its part, Foundayo will likely need to start generating around 22,000 prescriptions a week in order to hit current consensus forecasts of $160 million in second-quarter sales, RBC Capital Markets’ Trung ​Huynh said this week, as cited by Reuters. 

UPDATE: May 4, 2026

With three weeks of data on Lilly’s oral GLP-1 launch in obesity now on the books, the dimensions of Foundayo’s rollout—and its critical comparison to that of Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill—are coming into focus. 

In its third week on the U.S. market, which ended April 24, Foundayo generated some 5,600 prescriptions, analysts at Jefferies wrote in a May 1 note to clients. That level of adoption is numerically lower than the stats recorded by the Wegovy pill in its third week, when prescriptions for the oral obesity med came in at around 26,100, per the note. 

Nevertheless, almost all of Foundayo’s recorded performance stems from cash pay channels, according to the Jefferies team, with commercial access via insurance set to come online by the middle of this month, which will likely give Foundayo a substantial boost in uptake. 

The team acknowledged that Foundayo’s reimbursement “appears to be ramping more slowly vs oral Wegovy’s.” 

Overall, the analysts described Foundayo as “off to a solid start,” and estimate the drug will generate $146 million in the second quarter and $1.6 billion for all of 2026. That compares to consensus forecasts of $134 million and $1.2 billion, respectively. 

Lilly told the Jefferies team that, as of week three of its launch, some 45% of Foundayo prescriptions were coming through its direct-to-patient channel LillyDirect, alongside 35% of referrals from telehealth providers and the remaining 20% coming from traditional retail venues. 

During an earnings call with analysts last week, Lilly executives noted that there were around 20,000 patients on Foundayo in the U.S. The drug was approved April 1. 

As for Novo’s pill, oral Wegovy lassoed around 135,000 total prescriptions during the week that ended April 24, according to the Jefferies notes. 

UPDATE: April 24, 2026

Eli Lilly’s oral GLP-1 obesity treatment Foundayo has attracted 3,707 prescriptions though its second week on the market, lagging far behind the pace of Novo Nordisk’s GLP-1 pill Wegovy, which drew 18,410 prescriptions though its second week on the market in January. 

The results were made available by Jefferies from healthcare analytics firm IQVIA and are good through the week ending on April 17.

With the result, Lilly’s shares dipped by 4% on Friday, compared to a 7% gain for Novo.

Foundayo’s launch so far does compare favorably to that of Novo’s injected Wegovy, which numbered 1,578 prescriptions through two weeks when it reached the market in the U.S. but falls short of Lilly’s Zepbound pen, which counted 7,292 prescriptions through its second week.

In its note to investors, analysts from Jefferies called the result “disappointing vs. expectations."

Brand recognition has played a role, according to Bernstein analyst Courtney Breen, who said that online searches for GLP-1 drugs peaked during Wegovy’s launch, potentially boosting demand.

UPDATE: April 21, 2026

Eli Lilly’s oral GLP-1 Foundayo is off to a solid launch, drawing 1,390 prescriptions in its first week on the market, according to tracking figures from IQVIA and presented by Jefferies. The tabulation is from the week starting April 6. This compares to the 3,071 prescriptions Novo Nordisk garnered during its Wegovy pill launch week in January.

While Foundayo came up short in this oral GLP-1 launch week comparison, it did exceed the number of prescriptions recorded in the first week of the launch of both Lilly’s injected Zepbound (1,100) and Novo’s injected version of Wegovy (768).

In a note to clients, analysts with Jefferies cautioned that comparisons can be “tricky” given that oral Wegovy was launched at the start of the year and that initial capture rates from IQVIA are “volatile” and may not include product sampling. 

“Overall, we think Foundayo’s initial scripts look excellent,” the Jefferies team wrote, adding that it is modeling Foundayo’s sales to reach $1.6 billion this year, compared to a consensus of $1.5 billion, with its peak annual sales topping out at $30 billion versus the consensus of $26 billion. 

“We think the real opportunity for Foundayo is ex-U.S., given its clear advantages on scale, distribution and [cost of goods sold],” Jefferies wrote.

data.title: $200M in 5 weeks: Behind RevMed's 'eye-popping' Rasonque debut
data.description:
After roughly one month on the market, Revolution Medicines’ RAS inhibitor daraxonrasib is living up to its much-hyped potential, with an initial sales performance that more than one group of analysts considers “eye-popping.”

Still, with some temporary launch factors at play, RevMed leadership espoused a more cautiously optimistic viewpoint as it reported third-quarter earnings Wednesday. 

Following an Aug. 26 approval in patients with pretreated pancreatic adenocarcinoma, daraxonrasib—now known by the brand name Rasonque—delivered $197.6 million in sales for Q3, which ended on Sept. 30.

Analysts did not mince words about the stature of Rasonque’s early performance, with the team at Leerink Partners writing to clients that RevMed looks to be “pulling off the best oncology launch to date.” The nearly $200 million the drug secured in just a little over a month also comes well above the $80 million-to-$100 million haul the market had been priming for. 

The team at Jefferies, too, remarked that Rasonque’s sales came in more than twice that of “even the most bullish estimates,” now modeling $527 million in expected sales for the drug in the fourth quarter, a fair bit above the roughly $440 million now forecasted by Leerink. 

The team at Evercore ISI, for its part, claimed Rasonque’s debut was nothing short of “eye-popping.” The shop is now looking at a potential $500 million in Rasonque sales for the year’s final quarter, which it figures could segue into an expected $2.8 billion across 2027. 

While the sales performance to date is indeed “highly encouraging,” Anthony Mancini, RevMed’s chief global commercialization officer, took a measured approach in framing Rasonque’s future potential on a call with analysts. 

“With only five weeks of commercialization activity, it’s too early to draw conclusions about the normalized trajectory of launch,” he said, noting that expanded access switches and patients who’d been waiting for the therapy ahead of approval—both of which RevMed highlighted as prominent drivers of the rollout—represent “finite early launch dynamics.” 

“As our launch matures,” he said, “revenue will increasingly reflect ongoing treatment for newly eligible patients and ongoing treatment duration.” 

Related

FDA’s Rasonque review documents pressure RevMed as investors jitter over KRAS subgroup data

The U.S. rollout is nevertheless “off to a strong start,” Mancini said, reiterating RevMed’s priorities to provide a positive treatment experience, secure broad coverage and access and establish Rasonque as a new standard of care for the metastatic pancreatic cancer patients for whom the first-in-class drug is approved.

So far, the company is “encouraged by the progress we’re seeing against each of these priorities,” he added.

Overall, the drug’s sales haul reflects more than 5,000 patients treated in the U.S., coming over the course of just five weeks on the market.

That demand was threefold, according to Manicini. These include patients who are transitioning from RevMed’s U.S. expanded access program, a “sizable cohort” of patients who’d exhausted available treatment options by the time of approval and were “waiting for a new treatment option,” and new eligible patients starting on Rasonque in the wake of the FDA nod. 

The transition from the expanded access program to commercial supply has now wrapped up for U.S. patients, the commercialization chief said. 

Though the early launch factors Mancini highlighted no doubt gave Rasonque a boost in its initial debut, analysts seemed relatively assured that the RAS inhibitor is destined for a stellar sales run in the long-term. 

At Leerink, the team said they estimate that the population of new second-line patients accessing Rasonque was “also robust” in the third quarter. The analysts at Jefferies had a similar take, acknowledging the early bolus for Rasonque while nevertheless espousing continued confidence in what they framed as “‘organic’ demand” for the medicine.

A combination of strong science, transformative efficacy, high unmet need and successful execution by RevMed give Rasonque the potential to be “one of the best drug launches of all time,” the Jefferies team added. 

Still, RevMed leadership’s more cautious tone may have impacted confidence in the company’s stock, which was trading down more than 5% late Thursday morning. 

Rasonque has been much-ballyhooed ever since the drug’s data earned a standing ovation at the American Society of Clinical Oncology meeting in May, showing that it doubled progression-free survival following an earlier—and similarly impressive—overall survival victory in phase 3. 

With the green light, RevMed has also validated the broader RAS inhibition pathway, which had long been thought undruggable. The RAS protein is vital for the survival of many cancers, including most pancreatic cancers.

Elsewhere, RevMed is also gearing up to launch Rasonque in the European Union, where it won the blessing of the European Medicines Agency in October. 

Related

Lilly's obesity pill, RevMed's pancreatic cancer breakthrough among slew of CHMP endorsements in Europe

As the company waits on formal sign-off from the European Commission, launch prep and country-by-country reimbursement work is ongoing, Mancini said on RevMed’s call. 

While actual launch timing in Europe will depend on that Commission verdict and country-specific access accords, Mancini stressed that RevMed expects to be ready to launch as soon as its able overseas. The company is also working toward a swift rollout in Japan as Rasonque undergoes regulatory review there as well.

data.title: Alnylam seeks new commercial lead as Tanguler hits the exit
data.description:
Alnylam Pharmaceuticals is seeking a new chief commercial officer as the biopharma announced that its six-year CCO veteran Tolga Tanguler is leaving the company. 

No reason was given for his departure, and Tanguler did not offer a quote in the release.

The change appears to be immediate, and the company is now “working with an executive search firm to support the selection of its next Chief Commercialization Officer," per the announcement. Alnylam added that it "anticipates providing an update in due course."

Yvonne Greenstreet, M.D., CEO of Alnylam, thanked Tanguler for his tenure in a statement and said Alnylam under his guidance has “significantly expanded its global commercial organization and marketed portfolio, establishing a strong foundation for future growth.”

Thing have not however been going to plan on the commercial front this year. Alnylam’s stock plummeted 20% this week on its quarterly earnings release as sales of its pivotal commercial drug Amvuttra continued to disappoint analysts and investors. 

The RNA interference therapy was first approved in 2022 for polyneuropathy of hereditary transthyretin-mediated amyloidosis in adults and then in 2025 this was expanded to include certain patients with wild-type or hereditary transthyretin-mediated amyloidosis with cardiomyopathy.

Amvuttra’s sales, which are seen as key to Alnylam’s future, got off to a strong start but its trajectory has faltered this year, leading the company to cut guidance and weather major drops in its stock. 

Back in July, Alnylam’s stock price plummeted as much as 29% when it released its second quarter earnings that saw disappointing Amvuttra sales, leading to a lowered full-year forecast and triggering more fears over the transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTR) franchise.

Related

Alnylam shares tank 29% as Amvuttra disappoints with ATTR outlook cut for 2026

During its call to investors and journalists in that Q2, Tanguler spent quite some time on assuring investors that Amvuttra’s launch was progressing well and that the drug's long-term potential remained intact.

A similar story played out on October 29 during Alnylam's third quarter earnings. Amvuttra made $1.13 billion for the period, which was in line with Wall Street expectations, but this was apparently not enough to convince investors, who sent its stock down 20%.

William Blair analyst Myles Minter summed up the concerns in a note to clients: “The back-to-back quarters of headwinds undoubtedly call into question the growth outlook for the franchise and make it difficult to assess near-term 2027 revenue estimates as well as the longer-term trajectory.”

"As we look ahead, we have significant opportunities to reach more patients with our medicines, advance our pipeline and continue building a sustainable, high-performing business,” said Greenstreet in the release.

Alongside news of Tanguler's departure, Alnylam simultaneously announced a $1 billion share repurchase program. “Today’s repurchase authorization reflects our confidence in that future and our commitment to disciplined capital allocation,” explained Amy Schulman, chair of Alnylam's board, in a statement. 

“We are committed to continuing to evaluate opportunities to build on Alnylam’s strengths and create value for our shareholders."

data.title: Boehringer drives liver health education at NASCAR races
data.description:
There’s no speed limit on Boehringer Ingelheim’s efforts to spread liver health awareness. The company is hitting the track with race car driver Will Rodgers and his foundation to drive liver health advocacy around three NASCAR races this year. 

Boehringer’s team up with Rodgers and the Will Rodgers Liver Health Foundation sees the driver in the No. 53 Chevrolet for the Big Machine Racing team in three NASCAR O’Reilly Auto Parts Series (NOAPS) events this fall. Along with the “Driving Good Health” themed car, which is splashed in the Will Rodgers foundation colors, the campaign includes fan-zone activations and free liver screenings at the events. 

So far, the “Driving Good Health” program has posted up at NOAPS races at the Phoenix Raceway and the Talladega Superspeedway in October, with the Homestead-Miami Speedway event still to come on Nov. 6 through Nov. 8. There, those who stop by the “Driving Good Health” space can get non-invasive FibroScan liver assessments on site, provided by Echosens. Echosens’ FibroScan devices are the “gold standard” in quickly assesing liver fibrosis and steatosis. 

At the activation spot, Rodgers also shares with visitors his own experience with liver disease. The race car driver was diagnosed with the progressive liver disease primary sclerosing cholangitis at age three, and now uses “every lap to help people take care of their livers,” the foundation’s website explains. 

Boehringer joined forces with Rodgers to raise awareness about metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), which affects more than 13 million people in the U.S., and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), the less severe form of MASH. Announced during October’s Liver Health Awareness month, the program jumps on NASCAR’s national reach to give a wider platform to liver health education. 

MASH, a fatty liver disease, is a serious health concern that “often goes undiagnosed, and many people don’t realize they are at risk,” SVP of Boehringer’s obesity and liver health franchise Sylvia Shubert told Fierce. 

Related

AbbVie hits the gas on immunology awareness with McLaren F1 pact

“Through this collaboration, we have an opportunity to help people better understand liver health, learn more about the risk factors for MASH and encourage them to have informed conversations with their healthcare providers,” Shubert added. “By bringing education directly to communities through initiatives such as Driving Good Health, we hope to empower more people to take proactive steps toward understanding and managing their liver health and seek appropriate evaluation earlier to have the greatest impact on long-term health outcomes.”

The in-person activations at the races are meant to “meet people where they are,” Shubert said. 

Boehringer’s MASH awareness efforts are largely folded into its focus on metabolic diseases as it emphasizes the connection between liver health and overall metabolic health. The company explains the link in its “See Obesity, Think Liver” push, which shines a light on the liver’s role in obesity through educational material and spotlight visualizations encouraging clinicians to “see obesity differently" and include liver health assessments in obesity care. 

The company doesn’t yet have any approved MASH or obesity products, but its Zealand Pharma-partnered dual glucagon/GLP-1 receptor agonist survodutide holds an FDA breakthrough therapy designation in MASH and moderate or advanced fibrosis. The ongoing phase 3 program for the prospect is “set to redefine the treatment landscape,” head of human pharma Shashank Deshpande has said.  

As of now, the treatment landscape for MASH includes Novo’s Wegovy and Madrigal Pharmaceuticals’ Rezdiffra. Rezdiffra became the first FDA-approved product for MASH in 2024 and just crossed the $1 billion annual sales threshold this quarter, while Wegovy tacked on a MASH nod as its third indication last year. Madrigal has raised awareness for its treatment in an eye-catching educational tour featuring a giant inflatable liver that housed liver disease education within the 20-foot-tall organ. 

Meanwhile, Boehringer’s NASCAR marketing track is becoming a popular one for pharma awareness campaigns. AbbVie recently inked a multiyear deal with the McLaren Formula 1 team and launched its “Race to Innovate” campaign, which raises awareness of immune-mediated diseases and donates to global charities based on points McLaren earns. Last year, AstraZeneca and Zero Prostate Cancer sponsored NASCAR race cars at a pair of Memorial Day races, while Vanda Pharmaceuticals sponsored an IndyCar this summer to promote its motion sickness pill Nereus.

data.title: HCPs Aren’t Ignoring Your Science. They’re Ignoring How (and When) You Deliver It
data.description:
What did the investment deliver? It's one of the first questions leadership asks after every major congress, and for marketing teams it is rarely an easy one to answer.

Months of planning, faculty alignment and medical, legal and regulatory review sit behind a sizeable budget. It bought you one hour, in one room.

That hour competes with countless parallel sessions, and some of the specialists you most want to reach are elsewhere. Yet EMJ research found that nearly half of HCPs (47%) want to hear from industry before, during and after congress, so the opportunity for engagement shouldn’t end when the symposium does.

In fact, interest is strongest at precisely the point where many congress plans stop. The challenge is making sure your content reaches clinicians at each stage, and it captures their attention when it does.

Deliver beyond the room

You don’t need new content to make a congress investment work harder. The science is as relevant on Monday as it was on Friday in the congress hall, and because it is already approved, it is ready to travel. EMJ research shows where the appetite is:

  • 46% want post-event summaries
  • 41% want on-demand recordings
  • 30% want real-time highlights
  • 20% want pre-event previews


The two most popular formats both arrive after the session has ended.

Extend your reach to the right specialists

That leaves a ready-made audience: the specialists who stayed in clinic or chose a parallel session instead. The content has already been paid for, so every one of them reached after the congress lowers the cost per clinician engaged.

Reaching more clinicians only helps if they are the right ones, though. EMJ research into what motivates HCPs to open a medical email found:

  • 52% clinical relevance
  • 44% a trusted sender
  • 38% a personalised subject line


A specialist publisher such as EMJ ticks all three boxes: relevant evidence from a trusted source, targeted so a session reaches the right HCP at the right time. Whether they act on it depends on how it is presented.

Use format to win attention

Picture where post-congress content actually lands: on a phone checked between patients on a Monday morning, competing with a full inbox and a growing admin list. Whatever the format, it has minutes, not hours, to prove it is worth a clinician’s time.

Static formats can do that well. A symposium review, a simple infographic or a written summary published while the topic is current gives clinicians something clear to save, print or share.

However, interactive formats go further. When EMJ published the same articles in static and interactive versions, with identical evidence in both, the interactive versions delivered:

  • 3x more page views
  • 178% more sessions
  • 180% uplift in engaged sessions
  • 30% more interactions per user


The difference comes down to control: rather than scrolling past a block of text, clinicians can click, explore and answer their way through the same approved science. For example:

  • An interactive article where readers explore the data behind a finding
  • A patient case study with a clinical decision at each step
  • A video split into chapters so clinicians can navigate directly to what is most relevant to them


Interactive content has been EMJ’s highest-performing format for two consecutive years, and that work is earning industry recognition, with shortlistings at both The Drum Marketing Awards and the Marketing Week Awards in 2026.

Report on engagement, not just reach

Sends, opens and downloads show how far content travelled, but on their own they cannot show whether anyone engaged. The most useful reporting is built around the KPIs your team answers to, from engagement by specialty and therapy area to performance across a full campaign.

Interactive formats add another layer, because every click is a signal. You can see:

  • Which sections drew attention
  • Where readers dropped off
  • How clinicians answered knowledge checks


Static content, by contrast, can only tell you it was seen.

That is the answer leadership is really asking for: not “we published it”, but “here is what HCPs engaged with”. With that evidence in hand, the case for next year’s congress budget becomes far easier to make.

Four rules for maximising congress ROI

  • Reuse before you reinvest. Repurpose approved congress content before commissioning new assets.
  • Match format to purpose. Static for clear, accessible summaries; interactive for complex evidence.
  • Build for five minutes, not 50. Break content into short sections or chapters that fit around busy schedules.
  • Measure real engagement. Track what clinicians read, explore and complete, and use it to shape the next campaign.


The symposium bought you one hour, in one room. With the right plan, that hour is only the beginning.

data.title: Vanda drives straight into FDA trouble with fast-paced Nereus ad
data.description:
Vanda Pharmaceuticals’ action-packed TV ad for motion-sickness drug Nereus has irked the FDA, which accused (PDF) the company of creating a misleading impression of the drug’s safety and effectiveness. 

The animated ad shows a James Bond-esque car chase through a Mediterranean-style town and along a winding coastal road. A man in a white convertible chases a black sedan until he is forced to go another way. The three men in the black car get into a motorboat to escape, but two of them look unwell. 

Looking down from the bridge, the man in the white car sees them making their escape, pushes a button on the dashboard and swallows a black-and-white pill from the box that appears. The man, who the FDA said “appears satisfied and confident with his decision to take the capsule,” gets into another motorboat and speeds off across turbulent water. 

The FDA listed multiple ways in which the ad allegedly misstates the product’s safety and effectiveness. Because the man takes the pill following the car chase and just before getting in the motorboat, the ad creates the misleading impression that Nereus can be used after or immediately prior to engaging in activities that could lead to vomiting induced by motion, the FDA said. Nereus is taken as a preventive measure 60 minutes before a vomiting-inducing event, such as a boat trip. 

Vanda’s ad minimizes the risks associated with Nereus by “presenting visuals directly at odds” with the warnings and precautions section of the product information, the FDA said. The driving style depicted in the ad “requires acute mental awareness and an advanced state of alertness necessary to navigate the car and motorboat chase,” the agency said. Yet Nereus may impair physical or mental abilities needed to drive a car. The ad’s voiceover states that warning as the driver races along the coastal road.

The agency also outlined concerns that echo its criticisms of other ads over the past year. The ad fails to deliver the major statement concurrently using both audio and text, meaning it falls short of the need for the information to be presented in a clear, conspicuous and neutral manner, the FDA said. Similarly, the FDA ruled that the “riveting storyline” and visual style interfere with viewers’ ability to comprehend the major statement.

FDA staffers sent the untitled letter on Oct. 26 and gave Vanda 15 working days to respond in writing.

data.title: Merck eyes cancer-free finish line in new corporate campaign
data.description:
Merck & Co. is chasing the finish line with its eye on one prize: a world without cancer.

That’s the foundation of the company’s new corporate brand campaign, “From Our Pipeline to the Finish Line,” which recently debuted on its oncology-specific webpage and through in-person activations at the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) Congress in Madrid last month.

“We envision a future where more patients live longer and can move beyond cancer,” Merck says on the website. “That’s the finish line we’re working toward.”

The company doesn’t mince words. One in five people will develop cancer in their lifetime, and the disease remains a leading cause of death worldwide, Merck points out on the webpage. The site also lays out the company's oncology research priorities, pipeline and goal of delivering more than 10 cancer medicines by 2030.

Seeing the branding play out in Madrid was “really special,” Merck’s associate vice president of global communications, Courtney Ronaldo, said in an interview. According to Ronaldo, Merck’s pipeline is at “an inflection point right now,” with “one of the largest and most diverse pipelines in company history.”

To showcase the pipeline and highlight the “researchers and patients behind the research,” Ronaldo said, the company featured a series of videos on its website highlighting both patients and senior leaders.

In one video, four-time lung cancer survivor and patient advocate Terri Ann shares her journey through multiple cancer diagnoses and offers hope to patients by highlighting advancements in lung cancer care over the past decade, which have “changed everything.” For Terri Ann, the finish line she envisions is a day when lung cancer becomes a chronic disease “that we can all live with,” she said in the video.

In another “Finish Line” video, Marjorie Green, M.D., Merck's senior vice president and head of oncology global clinical development at Merck Research Laboratories, shares her hopes for the future. As Green speaks to the camera in a research lab setting, her voiceover plays over footage of patients, doctors and researchers wearing Merck lab coats, highlighting the company's role in advancing cancer care.

“There are multiple challenges in oncology,” Green acknowledges. “But I also look at them as opportunities.”

Green also discusses Merck’s research priorities, using specific but accessible language to describe her vision for a future of cancer care centered on personalized therapies based on the genetics of a patient’s tumor. Like Terri Ann, she wishes for a future in which people “don’t view cancer as a death sentence, but as another condition that can be controlled and treated just like any other disease that’s out there.”

Related

Girding against Keytruda cliff, Merck splits oncology into standalone business unit

The campaign's hero video brings together the patient and company perspectives in a fast-paced, action-filled 60 seconds.

“Cancer is life interrupted,” a gruff voiceover says. “Plans put on hold. Life measured in appointments, scans, and treatment decisions. Every day a race against uncertainty. At Merck, we’re in a race to outsmart cancer.”

His words are accompanied by quick flashes of oncology imagery, including brain scans and wheels racing across a hospital floor. The emotionally intense footage then shifts to brighter scenes inside Merck's labs, featuring automated equipment, focused researchers and microscopic cancer visualizations.

“Behind every data point is a patient waiting for better options,” the voiceover says, as Terri Ann briefly appears on-screen. Scenes of happier moments, including a patient ringing a hospital bell, hugging family members and celebrating birthdays, provide a stark contrast to the grimmer opening footage. “From our pipeline to the finish line, Merck is here.”

In making the video, Merck "wanted to make sure it was really upbeat and really conveyed the momentum and the advances that we've had in oncology,” Ronaldo explained.

The “Finish Line” theme extends to social media, including a video featuring Eliav Barr, M.D., Merck Research Laboratories' head of global clinical development and chief medical officer, posted on his LinkedIn account. In the video, Barr discusses what “From Our Pipeline to the Finish Line” means to him, echoing language from the website, including “our research has rewritten medical textbooks.”

While the other videos conclude with the Merck logo, Barr's video features the MSD logo, reflecting the company's global identity. Merck operates under the MSD name outside the U.S. and Canada.

The company plans to continue expanding the digital rollout and may extend the campaign to other therapeutic areas in 2027, Ronaldo said. As an umbrella campaign, the initiative can help ensure a “consistent presence” for Merck across therapeutic areas and “show our leadership and research across the board,” she added.

“We’ve been around for a very long time, and R&D is really the cornerstone of what we pride ourselves in at the company,” Ronaldo said. “We do invest heavily in R&D as a company, and we really take pride in that kind of approach and that kind of being our reputation, putting a lot of scientific rigor around our pipeline,” she said.

Given that R&D focus, the “pipeline to finish line” phrasing felt like a “unique space for Merck to own,” Ronaldo explained. “It’s a really authentic campaign for our company and where we’re at right now.”

In Madrid, ESMO was packed with headline-making developments, including an unexpected leak that prompted Merck and Moderna to release highly anticipated phase 3 cancer vaccine results ahead of schedule.

Even if Merck wasn't top of mind for conference attendees upon arrival, its campaign was hard to miss. Digital signage greeted travelers at the airport, while the company's advertising presence extended to buses and billboards throughout Madrid, as well as the conference itself, Ronaldo said.

“We’re speaking from a place of leadership and not necessarily like a brand objective or brand name,” she said, noting that the umbrella campaign could appear at future medical conferences.

Merck's oncology portfolio has long been defined by megablockbuster Keytruda, which generated $31.7 billion in sales alongside Keytruda Qlex last year, accounting for more than half of the company's annual pharmaceutical revenue.

With Keytruda's loss of exclusivity approaching, Merck has been investing heavily in its pipeline to drive future growth. CFO Caroline Litchfield described 2027 as “another year of investment” during the company's recent third-quarter earnings call.

CEO Rob Davis has also pointed to the “broadest and widest pipeline we’ve had in years,” outlining opportunities for future growth that could generate more than $70 billion in annual revenue by the mid-2030s.

data.title: Sanofi runs emotive RSV campaign
data.description:
Would you know the difference between a normal cold and one that has turned into something more serious? Sanofi is raising awareness of bronchiolitis, a potential complication of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in young children, with a new a tough-to-watch PSA video. 

In what the French Big Pharma dubbed an “immersive experiment,” the video opens with a mother walking toward a crib overlaid with the sounds of a baby struggling to breathe with a wet-sounding, raspy cough. 

Several parents were brought into the room one-by-one, with the sound playing on a speaker (the prerecording is not from a real child and there are no children used in the video) and asked, “what does this sound mean to you?” 

The sound, which is usually accompanied by the child’s chest sucking inward, is that of bronchiolitis, a chest infection that can arise in some children due to a progressing RSV infection. 

It is the leading cause of hospitalization in infants under one and can advance from a typical cold into a deeper infection over several days, leading to problems breathing and feeding. 

The first mother says it “sounds like a cough” but that “a doctor needs to check on it.” The second mother talks haltingly and with high emotion about her daughter Lea previously having RSV and says, “I know this sound.” This is echoed by a father who comes in and says, “it brings back quite difficult memories.” 

Related

Sanofi enlists another celeb mom in actress Keke Palmer to spread the Beyfortus word

France-based pediatrician Dr. Fabienne Chan Sellem then comes in saying parents should always talk to their doctor about any worrying symptoms, such as the sounds of those rasping coughs. 

Sanofi, alongside AstraZeneca, currently markets Beyfortus, a drug that is designed to help stop RSV turning into bronchiolitis in children. The protective antibody shares the first-season infant market with Merck’s Enflonsia. 

Beyfortus has however seen declining sales in the past year, and Sanofi will be hoping this latest awareness push can help boost sales for the new RSV season. 

In Sanofi's third quarter financials released in late October, Beyfortus revenue fell 15.4% to €631 million. Much of the drop was driven by the U.S., where the drug generated €240 million, down 39.3% year-over-year. This was partially offset by stronger uptake in Europe and other global markets. 

Sanofi has been going all in on Beyfortus marketing. Back in September, it brought in some celebrity mom star power to help spread the word about its pediatric antibody.

For that spot, Emmy Award-winning actress, singer and TV host Keke Palmer teamed up with Sanofi as a paid spokesperson, joining actor and singer Mandy Moore, author Elaine Welteroth, chef Gaby Dalkin, citizen astronaut Katya Echazarreta and gold-medal Olympic gymnast Shawn Johnson East, all of whom also have teamed up with Sanofi for its RSV messaging.

But Sanofi’s promotions for the drug have not all gone to plan this year. In the summer, Sanofi got in hot water with the U.K. marketing watchdog the PMCPA, which reprimanded the pharma for using “a highly misleading interpretation of data” to make disparaging claims about Pfizer’s RSV vaccine.

It also earned the ire of the FDA in the same week in July, with the U.S. regulator calling out Sanofi’s promotion of Beyfortus in an untitled letter that took issue with the company’s characterization of the med as a general RSV preventative.
